However, most prior work in dexterous manipulation focuses on single, isolated tasks. In contrast, our key insight is that these multi-step manipulation tasks require resource-aware grasps where the robot must conserve fingers for later actions rather than simply optimizing an initial whole-hand grasp in isolation. We introduce HANDFUL, a learning framework that treats finger usage as a limited resource and rewards the robot for exploring one- and two-finger grasps that leave fingers and in-hand space available for downstream tasks. These grasps are then efficiently selected and trained for downstream tasks via curriculum-based policy learning We further propose HANDFUL-Bench, a simulation benchmark that introduces sequential dexterous manipulation tasks across multiple second-subtask objectives, including pushing, pulling, and pressing, under a shared grasp + second objective setup. Second objectives include: pushing another object, pressing a button, twisting a knob, pulling a drawer, and grasping a second object. Results show that resource-aware grasp planning improves both success rate and robustness compared to a baseline that greedily optimizes the initial grasp before attempting the second subtasks. We additionally validate our approach on a real dexterous hand. Together, this work establishes resource-aware grasp planning as a key principle for multi-step dexterous manipulation. Supplementary material is available on our website: [handfuldex.github.io] (http://handful-dex.github.io).

title: Inafa'maolek Archaeologies: CHamoru heritage resurgence amidst U.S. militarization on Guahan (Guam)
abstract: The rise of U.S. militarization on Guam and the passage of federal laws governing cultural resource management and environmental protection have rapidly increased archaeological surveying over the last few decades. This research investigates the role of CHamorus, the Indigenous people of Guam and the Mariana Islands, who work as archaeologists and historic preservationists to steward Indigenous cultural heritage amidst military build-up. These applied anthropologists play a crucial role in protecting CHamoru heritage, working with archaeological materials spanning up to 4,000 years old that connect present day CHamorus to ancient ancestors. Using ethnographic methods, including participant observation and semi-structured interviews, this research examines how CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists are incorporating CHamoru knowledge systems throughout their work on their ancestral homelands, focusing on the newly constructed Marine Corps Camp Blaz base. This research maps the current institutional landscape of heritage management on Guam, identifying some of the challenges of CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists within their work. For these practitioners, archaeology has been utilized as a site of resistance towards colonial knowledge production on the CHamoru people. Drawing on Indigenous and activist archaeological literature, this research explores how CHamoru practitioners are subsequently navigating Indigenous identity, community, and place-making as they work on specific heritage sites. By centering CHamoru relationships to land and prioritizing community access, CHamoru practitioners in the field are utilizing archaeology as a tool to foster sovereignty through decolonial heritage education, while simultaneously mobilizing to protect Indigenous cultural landscapes amidst violent militarization.

title: Decoding Cave Wall Patterns to Search for Life Elsewhere
abstract: Caves on Mars and the Moon suggest that similar environments on Earth can help scientists search for signs of life beyond our planet. One promising avenue of research is focused on "biovermiculations" - worm-like patterns of microbe-rich material that form on cave walls. Most studies of these features come from sulfur-rich caves, where microbes drive their formation through sulfur-based chemistry. This study examines biovermiculations in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky, a limestone cave with different environmental conditions, to better understand how they form and whether they are truly biological in origin. Our hypothesis is that biovermiculations in non-sulfur caves are shaped by active microbial processes. We combined microscopy, spatial mapping, and DNA analysis techniques to analyze these patterns. In Mammoth Cave, biovermiculations appear across five distinct morphologies and are made from materials like soot, mud, and cricket guano. Their form is influenced more by the type and behavior of available material than by nearby patterns. Microscopy revealed motile microorganisms that could actively rearrange material on cave surfaces. We also found that these features have developed over at least the past century, growing into 19-20th century soot deposits but not significantly affecting newer ones (post-1970). Genetic analyses show that the microbial communities within biovermiculations are distinct from other sites and share similar compositions across samples. Many of these microbes are associated with sulfur and iron cycling, as well as methane use, suggesting diverse metabolic activity. These findings help refine how scientists identify signs of life in cave-like environments on other planets.

title: My Tutor Bot: Integrating Large Language Models into Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Fundamental Programming
abstract: This research explores how integrating large language models (LLMs) into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) can enhance student learning outcomes in fundamental programming courses. Building on findings that combining computer-based and human tutoring is highly effective, this study examines how LLMs can replicate the benefits of human tutors, such as personalized feedback and scaffolding, while offering scalable, adaptive support. To investigate this, I implemented "My Tutor Bot" within Northwestern's Comp Sci 211 across Winter and Spring Quarters 2026, creating a trustworthy, instructor-controlled environment by training the LLM exclusively on Professor Zhang and Hummel's course materials. If a student has any questions beyond the scope of the provided course materials, My Tutor Bot informs them that it cannot respond. My Tutor Bot is also FERPA-compliant and built to protect students' privacy. This ensures a safe space for students to explore content and receive 24/7 adaptive scaffolding tailored to the curriculum. By analyzing chat logs, interviews, and surveys, the research evaluates the impact of targeted AI tutoring on conceptual understanding, student engagement, and educational equity. The results aim to identify best practices for leveraging AI in academic settings and provide insights into how LLM-driven ITS can close equity gaps and improve learning outcomes in STEM fields.

title: Auditory Processing and Behavioral Responses to Sound During Sleep
abstract: Sleep has traditionally been viewed as a state of sensory disconnection, but past studies have found that the brain continues to process external stimuli across sleep stages, with sensory responses maintained during REM sleep. Prior research also found that behavioral responses to auditory lexical-decision tasks can occur during sleep, but most participants do not recall these interactions upon awakening unless they experience lucid dreams. In this study, we investigated when external sounds become incorporated into dreams and whether real-time behavioral responses can occur without conscious awareness. Participants were trained to associate five distinct sounds with specific sniffing patterns. These cues were presented during N2, N3, and REM sleep, followed by awakenings after delays of 0.5, 3, or 10 seconds to collect dream reports and assess recall. Across 78 analyzed awakenings, participants were able to volitionally respond to external stimuli during sleep through sniffing responses. Among these awakenings, 16 total incorporation trials were observed: 5 during N2 sleep, 2 during N3 sleep, and 9 during REM sleep. This suggests that REM may be the most receptive stage for integrating external stimuli into dream content. Overall, these findings show that the sleeping brain can respond to external stimuli in real time. This work has implications for applications in dream research, memory consolidation, and sleep-based interventions.

title: Infants Can Reason About Objects Even When They Are Hidden: Evidence from Containment Events
abstract: Before infants can speak, hearing an object (e.g., my cat) named influences how they represent it-as an individual ("Misty") or a category member (CAT). These distinct representations affect infants' memory: when an object is named with a distinct name, but not a category name, infants encode that object as a unique individual and distinguish it from other objects. Here, we ask whether naming objects also has downstream consequences for infants' reasoning about the objects in dynamic events. In two ongoing experiments, 12- and 16-month-olds (planned N=96) participate via Zoom. All infants are full-term and primarily English-exposed. In Experiment 1, infants first see videos of four plush bunnies that differ only in color, and each bunny is labeled with a distinct novel noun. Then, in the test videos, the last-named bunny (blue bunny) is hidden inside a small container and then retrieved after a pause. In the nochange event, the same-colored bunny is retrieved. In the change event, a different colored bunny (pink bunny) is retrieved. Experiment 2 is identical to Experiment 1, except the four bunnies are first labeled with the same name. We expect infants to look longer at the test event they find unexpected. Preliminary results revealed that infants looked longer at the change than the nochange event in Experiment 1, suggesting that both 12- and 16-month-olds successfully reasoned about the individual bunnies when they had distinct names. This work extends prior work to reveal new insights about infants' early link between language and cognition.

title: Method Matters: Including Critical Race Theory in the Academic Tradition of Qualitative Meaning Making
abstract: Critical Race Theory (CRT) recognizes race as a social construct. It examines and acknowledges how race is embedded in policies, institutions, and social structures. The current social and political climate asserts that racism shouldn't be interrogated, and the lived experiences of people of color aren't mediated by race. As a result, Critical Race Theory has been under attack and delegitimized as a credible research framework. However, utilizing CRT as a framework and analytical lens in qualitative research allows for rich and diverse stories to be expressed. Specifically analyzing the case study methodology, which is a detailed examination of an event or phenomenon, this study worked to understand how CRT can be used in case studies and inform the narratives that can be communicated. To investigate, I created research outlines, conducted a literature review, and completed annotated bibliographies on CRT and its application in case studies. I discovered that using CRT in case studies isolates and highlights race to uncover the impacts of race and racism on people of color's lives, validating people of color's experiences with racism. As racism continues to affect people of color negatively, understanding how race shapes lived experience is essential for driving meaningful policy and structural reform. This research has direct implications for how race-centered studies and research involving people of color are designed and conducted. Further development of CRT within qualitative research methodologies is warranted to deepen meaning-making and expand the range of stories that academic research can share.

title: Cortical Interneurons in the Mouse Model of Fragile X
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects how people communicate, learn, and interact with the world, and it impacts more than 1% of people globally. One of the most common inherited causes of ASD is Fragile X syndrome, which occurs when the FMR1 gene is turned off. Researchers believe that many ASD symptoms may result from an imbalance between excitatory brain signals, which increase activity, and inhibitory signals, which calm activity down. In Fragile X syndrome, this imbalance may be caused by the loss or reduced function of inhibitory brain cells called interneurons. This project investigates whether the death or dysfunction of these interneurons in early development contributes to this imbalance. Using a mouse model of Fragile X syndrome, we focus on the somatosensory cortex, the part of the brain that processes sensory information such as touch. Specifically, we study parvalbumin- and somatostatin-containing interneurons, which help regulate brain activity and are critical for normal circuit development. To track these cells, we use genetically modified mice in which interneurons luminesce red under fluorescent microscopy. Brain tissue is collected at key stages of early postnatal development, sectioned, and imaged to count interneurons and inhibitory synapses across different layers of the cortex. Additional staining methods allow us to measure markers of inhibitory connections. By comparing Fragile X mice to healthy controls, we aim to determine whether reduced interneuron survival helps explain cortical hyperexcitability in ASD. Identifying when and where these changes occur could guide future therapies designed to restore healthy brain circuit balance in autism.

title: Developing a cFos Atlas to map brain activity
abstract: Light plays a critical role in regulating physiological and behavioral processes, yet the neural circuits underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) contribute to functions such as circadian photoentrainment, mood regulation, and thermoregulation, and project broadly throughout the brain, mapping their downstream signaling pathways is essential for understanding how light impacts brain function. This project aimed to investigate how ipRGCs influence brain-wide activity by developing a c-Fos-based activity atlas. C-Fos, an immediate early gene, was used in order to detect the areas of the brain that are activated upon light exposure. To accomplish this, two groups of mice were used: a control group maintained in darkness and an experimental group exposed to a brief light pulse. Following stimulation, brains were extracted, coronally sectioned, and processed using immunohistochemistry to label c-Fos. Additional markers, including NeuN and ChAT, were used to identify neuronal populations. Fluorescent imaging enabled visualization of activity patterns across brain regions. The resulting dataset provides a foundational framework for constructing a whole-brain c-Fos atlas of lightresponsive activity, revealing distinct regions activated in response to ipRGC stimulation. This work establishes a reference map that can be used to compare activity patterns in future studies, including models lacking ipRGC function, to better define the role of these cells in neural circuits. Ultimately, this research advances a systems-level understanding of how light influences brain function and behavior, with broader implications for circadian biology and mood-related disorders.

title: When Silence Speaks: Comparing Conversational Delays in Schizophrenia and Depression
abstract: Psychosis is a mental health condition in which an individual exhibits severe impairments in the ability to discern between what is real and what is not. While psychosis is generally known for presenting as hallucinations and delusions, a growing body of literature has also identified speech abnormalities in psychotic patients, characterized by lulls in conversational turn-taking. More specifically, these individuals tend to have extended pauses before answering questions. Our research aims to extend these findings by differentiating delays in response latency between individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) and those at clinical high-risk (CHR) for psychosis. These findings could be used to assess potential differences in symptomatology in order to better distinguish early-warning signs of psychosis from other mood disorders. Through retrospective analysis of clinical interviews, our team has categorized speech patterns to investigate whether response latency differs significantly between MDD and CHR populations. Observed differences in turn-taking delays may be indicative of distinct underlying mechanisms in social functioning and could support conversational turn-taking as a behavioral biomarker for assessing psychotic risk. This could have major implications in improving early detection of psychosis by enabling timely intervention and thereby optimizing long-term clinical outcomes.

title: PRL2 and the PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling pathways in T-ALL
abstract: T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive blood cancer that comprises 10-13% of leukemia diseases in children. Certain signaling pathways, such as the PI3K/PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in these T-ALL cancer cells are switched on and promote the progression of the disease. Many of these pathways are controlled by oncogenes such as PRL2 (Phosphatase of Regenerating Liver 2), which are proteins that promote unregulated cell division and growth that are characteristic of cancer cells. This project aims to determine if PRL2 promotes cancer growth by disabling the PTEN tumor suppressor and therefore activating the PI3K/PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. To investigate this signaling pathway, we sequenced for different conditional mouse models to observe the interactions of these proteins: PRL2 -/- (KO), PTEN WT; PRL2 -/- (KO), PTEN +/- (F/+); PRL2 +/+ (WT), PTEN WT; PRL2 +/+ (WT), PTEN +/- (F/+). By isolating and analyzing the DNA sequences offetal mouse livers, we created four different groups of mice DNA with different genetic combinations, including mice that lacked the PRL2 protein (knockout mice, KO). Creating these conditional groups of mice allows us to isolate the mechanisms of PRL2 and how it influences the spread and severity of disease. Knockout of PRL2 allows us to determine if PTEN regains function and reduces overall disease progression in mice and the mechanisms behind it. We hope our findings will help us determine a new way to prevent cancer growth through targeted therapies, leading to better survival rates and treatments for pediatric T-ALL cases.

title: How Crm1 Brings Genes to the Nuclear Edge-and the Proteins That Help It
abstract: Cells regulate gene activity not only through molecular signals but also by physically organizing DNA within the nucleus. Recent research suggests that genes positioned near structures called nuclear pores can become more active. A protein called Crm1, best known for transporting molecules out of the nucleus, also helps bring genes to these locations, acting as a docking factor that influences gene activity. However, the additional factors required for this process remain unknown. Crm1 is also frequently overactive in human cancers, but the mechanisms underlying its role in disease are not fully understood. This project aims to identify proteins that cooperate with Crm1 in controlling gene positioning and activity. Using a yeast model system, mutations are introduced throughout the genome and compared between normal cells and cells with elevated levels of Crm1. Mutations that reduce the harmful effects of excess Crm1 are analyzed to identify candidate proteins involved in this pathway. This work aims to uncover the network of factors that enable Crm1 to position genes at the nuclear periphery, providing new insight into how spatial organization influences gene expression. Understanding this mechanism may help explain how disruptions in nuclear organization contribute to diseases such as cancer.

title: Black Players, White Schools: How integration reshaped Southern college football
abstract: The landscape of college football has long been shaped by unequal access to power, resources, and visibility, yet one sector of programs remains consistently overlooked: historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). This paper challenges the common narrative of integration as a straightforward success story by revealing how it reproduced new forms of inequality within the sport. Understanding this dynamic not only reframes the history and temporality of college football but also helps explain the persistent disparities in funding, exposure, and institutional power that continue to shape the game today. In my research, I argue that the integration of college football in the 1960s and 1970s, particularly in the South, did not benefit the Black community; it actually harmed it. Integration reshaped the sport in ways that pulled talent, money, and attention away from historically Black colleges and universities and concentrated them towards predominantly white institutions (PWIs). Drawing on a combination of academic sports scholarship and primary sources, including Black newspapers and collegiate publications, my research uses a chronological and comparative analysis to trace how integration unfolded across regions and institutions. By examining key case studies, including the rise of HBCU programs, the structure of segregated PWI football, and pivotal moments such as the integration of major Southern powerhouses, the paper shows how success by integrated teams prompted PWIs to recruit Black athletes for competitive advantage rather than moral progress. This shift concentrated visibility and resources within already dominant programs, weakening the institutional and cultural centrality of HBCU football.

title: Novel Strategies for Assessing Awareness in the Borderlands between Sleep and Wake
abstract: Our study aims to exploit lucid dreaming, the state of being aware of dreaming while in a dream, to investigate the threshold between wake and sleep. The goal of the study is for napping participants to provide signals about their experience in response to auditory cues during sleep-onset, the period when the body transitions into sleep. Part of the challenge for participants is to retain memory of their experiences after awakening. Electrodes for monitoring sleep physiology are applied to participants' scalp and face. Prior to a 90-minute nap, participants listened to a 3-beep cue while cultivating mental clarity of being aware of the present moment. These cues were presented again during sleep to reactivate that mental clarity, so that participants could signal about their subjective state. They were instructed to frown to indicate feeling asleep or smile to indicate feeling awake. Participants were awoken periodically to provide a report of their experience and complete a standard set of questions. EEG data were analyzed to determine participants' sleep stage. Data collection is ongoing, and so far 62 trials have been completed on 5 participants. Out of these 62 trials, in 7 (11%), an awake participant reported feeling asleep and in 12 (19%), a sleeping participant reported feeling awake. This provides evidence for the prevalence of sleepstate misperception, in which participants incorrectly perceive whether they are asleep or awake. These results open the door to asking more about why awareness does not always line up with objective sleep state.

title: Functionalizing Yarns with Dip Coating for Smart Knitted Haptic Tactile Interfaces
abstract: The human skin is lined with several mechanoreceptors that are constantly converting things like pressure, vibration and textures into tactile signals that our brain can interpret. Replicating a small portion of this sensitivity into everyday materials would make sensing possible without being intrusive. Clothes are almost all knitted and universally needed by everyone, which makes it the perfect choice to begin embedding sensing into what we use. However, the process is limited by the material as there are no commercially available conductive yarns that are machine knittable, flexible, and insulated in a way that can be useful for research and prototyping. This project addresses this problem by developing a low-cost dip coating process that produces custom insulated conductive yarns compatible with knitting machines. We studied the effects that varying mechanical, chemical, and environmental parameters had on coating uniformity, thickness, and electrical isolation. By characterizing this behavior, we have developed a fabrication process that meets all requirements for being integrated into everyday knitted items. The initial results of these custom yarns have been tested in a proper knitting machine which proved the abrasion resistance was enough to maintain proper electrical insulation after being used to knit. These knitted items were used to create capacitive sensing pressure arrays that mimic mechanoreceptors and triboelectric nanogenerators for low power embedded systems. These results demonstrate that by solving the yarn fabrication problem, a new class of embedded smart knitted textiles applications can be created, from haptic feedback interfaces to pose tracking for AI databases.

title: Optimization of Carbon Black in Conversion Cathodes: Investigation of Additive Impurities
abstract: The growing environmental concerns associated with fossil fuels have driven demand for sustainable energy alternatives, the adoption of electric vehicles, and the decarbonization of the electric grid. In order to support this transition, there is an increasing need for more energy-dense lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) to support electrification. A typical battery consists of three main components: the anode, cathode, and electrolyte, with the cathode composed of an cathode active material, conductive additive, and binder. While conventional cathodes rely on cobalt- or nickelbased intercalation materials, these face supply risks and are nearing their theoretical capacity limits. Conversion cathodes are a promising alternative which offers 200300% higher energy density than traditional intercalation cathodes. Here, we study FeF2 conversion cathodes, which have been extensively studied due to their high energy density, low cost, and mineral abundance. However, due to low electronic conductivity, conversion cathodes require ~30% conductive additive, whereas intercalation cathodes typically achieve ~90% active mass loading. To overcome this, my research involved optimizing carbon black conductive additives by investigating their composition, electrochemical performance, and impurities. Commercial and impurity-rich carbon blacks were analyzed using galvanostatic cycling and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) to investigate the effect of impurity concentration on cycling performance. It was demonstrated that Li-ion halfcells fabricated using sulfur-rich carbon black samples suffered a loss of long-term cycle stability. These results suggest that controlling impurity chemistry in conductive additives is crucial for the overall performance of Li-ion batteries.

title: Say what again? Investigating the intelligibility of Formula 1 driver speech between situations, contexts, and language backgrounds
abstract: This study investigated how background noise and speaker characteristics affect intelligibility in real-world contexts, specifically by using naturally occurring speech samples from Formula 1 drivers in different race-related situations. Thus, this study extends controlled laboratory-based research on speech-in-noise recognition to a naturally occurring, high-stakes communicative situation. We compiled a corpus of 630 utterances from 21 Formula 1 drivers (9 first-language English speakers, 12 second-language English speakers) across three acoustic environments: studio interviews (minimal noise), paddock interviews (moderate noise), and race communications (high noise). Utterances from 4 first-language English speakers and 4 second-language English speakers then were selected to form the experimental stimulus set. 51 first-language English-speaking listeners (ages 22–81) transcribed 96 experimental utterances (8 speakers × 3 noise conditions × 4 utterances) in a web-based task. Participants were randomly assigned to either see contextual question prompts while listening to each utterance or transcribe utterances without contextual support. Transcriptions were scored using Autoscore, an automated scoring software (Borrie et al., 2019). Results revealed substantial effects of background noise, speaker native language status, and contextual support on intelligibility. Intelligibility increased progressively from race to paddock to studio conditions. Participants correctly transcribed utterances from first-language English speakers at a higher rate than second-language English speakers. Contextual prompts improved intelligibility, with benefits increasing as noise levels increased. These findings reveal the compounded communication challenges in Formula 1 and, by extension, other real-world speech communication situations where speakers must communicate in their second language while contending with extreme acoustic degradation during high-pressure situations.

title: AI-Assisted Validation of Transfer Data in Economic Research
abstract: Largescale economic research increasingly relies on structured datasets compiled from hundreds of academic papers. However, extracting and validating this information remains a major challenge due to inconsistent reporting formats, ambiguous variable definitions, and the need for manual interpretation. These issues introduce errors and significantly slow down the research process, particularly in metaanalyses of global poverty interventions. Accurate extraction of transfer amounts is especially important, yet papers report values in local currency (LCU), nominal USD (NUSD), or purchasing power parity (PPP), making manual validation timeconsuming and prone to human error. This project addresses these challenges by developing an AIassisted system to audit key financial variables in cash transfer studies. Using structured prompting and automated workflows, the system extracts planned transfer amounts directly from research papers and compares them to preexisting values stored in a centralized dataset. For any selected variable (xfer\_amt\_pln\_lcu, xfer\_amt\_pln\_nusd, or xfer\_amt\_pln\_ppp), the pipeline generates four subcolumns: the original spreadsheet value, the AIextracted value, a match/mismatch assessment, and the supporting quote from the paper. This structure enables systematic validation across studies and reduces reliance on manual verification. Developing this system required integrating AI coding agents, resolving Google authentication issues, and debugging cases where Codex returned incorrect values. Testing in the metadata audit sandbox demonstrates that the system reliably identifies agreement and disagreement between sources, highlighting both data inconsistencies and limitations in automated interpretation. By automating a previously manual and errorprone process, this project strengthens the reliability of transfer amount metadata and contributes to GPRL's broader effort to build scalable, AIassisted validation tools for development economics research.

title: Effects of Systemic Inflammation on Neuronal Activity in Transgenic Alzheimer's Mice using c-fos
abstract: Understanding the interplay between Alzheimer's Disease (AD) pathology and systemic inflammation is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms underlying acute disorders of cognition such as delirium. We therefore employed a multifaceted approach to investigate the effects of systemic inflammation on neuronal activity in brain slices in a transgenic AD mouse model (5xFAD and TauP301S) We studied 5xFAD transgenic mice overexpressing amyloid, TauP301S transgenic mice, with their Tau tangles, and their respective wild-type (WT) siblings. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) from E. coli (0.5 mg/kg) induced systemic inflammation, while a control group received a saline injection. To quantify activity in mouse brains, we used c-Fos, an immediate early gene, as the marker for neuronal activity in brain tissue. We performed immunohistochemistry on brain slices using the DAB reaction to analyze c-Fos+ cells in multiple regions of interest involved in delirium pathophysiology. Preliminary home-cage behavioral analysis revealed and validated that systemic inflammation suppressed spontaneous locomotion in these mice, disrupting typical circadian rhythms and being more evident in dark periods. The imaged slices for the experimental groups are currently being analyzed via QuPath - a quantitative pathology software. Preliminary data analysis have revealed significant effects of substance, especially within cortical areas. Further statistical analysis is ongoing to evaluate potential differential sensitivities between 5xFAD, TauP301S and WT mice to these manipulations.

title: Fingerprinting Carbon Capture: Tracing Enhanced Rock Weathering Through Soil with Strontium Isotopes and Alkalinity
abstract: Limiting global climate change requires not only reducing greenhouse gas emissions but also verifying carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategies at statistically significant scales. Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is a CDR strategy that accelerates the dissolution of silicate minerals in soils, converting atmospheric CO2 into stable aqueous alkalinity. As interest in ERW grows, accurately verifying carbon capture and distinguishing silicate-derived products from other sources has become a central challenge. Alkalinity measurements are widely used to quantify weathering-driven CO2 removal, but they are not source-specific and may reflect inputs from carbonates, fertilizers, or background soil processes. Current data show that basalt-amended systems produce elevated and stable alkalinity, with mean values of 28,940 3,020 mg/L compared to 25,480 2,870 mg/L in controls over a 13-month storage period, indicating minimal temporal variability; however, these measurements alone cannot confirm silicate-derived carbon capture. Combining radiogenic strontium isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) measured through a thermal ionization mass spectrometer with alkalinity measurements enables source-specific tracing of ERW processes through soil profiles. Depth-resolved analyses may reveal that basalt-amended soils exhibit distinct unradiogenic isotopic signatures alongside increased alkalinity, indicating mobilization of silicate-derived weathering products. These findings demonstrate that integrating isotopic tracers with aqueous chemistry improves ERW verification by linking geochemical signals directly to mineral sources, strengthening carbon accounting, and supporting the deployment of scalable soil-based climate solutions.

title: Centralizing Search: How AI-Generated Summaries on Search Engine Results Pages Reshape User Engagement and Perception
abstract: The integration of generative AI into search interfaces is shifting user attention from multi-source exploration toward reliance on a single synthesized response. This study examines how interface type (AI summary vs. traditional link-based) influences landing page engagement, article access patterns, and perceptual outcomes, including credibility, trust, and satisfaction, and whether these effects vary by search topic (health vs. pop culture). Using a 2 x 2 between-subjects design with 48 undergraduate participants, we find that AI summary interfaces significantly increase time spent on the landing page-by 3.5 times in the health domain and by 2.1 times in the pop culture domain-suggesting a shift toward more centralized attention. However, effects on downstream behaviors and perceptual outcomes are limited. Article access patterns are driven more by task domain than by interface type, with pop culture participants accessing more sources than health participants across conditions. We find no clear evidence that interface type influences perceived credibility or trust. At the same time, health content is rated as more credible than pop culture content regardless of interface, consistent with domain-based epistemic expectations. For satisfaction, a significant interaction emerges: traditional interfaces produce substantial variation across topics, whereas AI interfaces reduce variability, yielding more consistent - though not necessarily higher - user experiences. Taken together, these findings suggest that AI summaries centralize attention and standardize user experience, shifting search from exploratory engagement toward more uniform modes of information consumption.

title: Electrically Tunable Structural Color in Photonic Crystal Films of PEDOT:PSS-SiO2 for Electrochromic Devices
abstract: Electrochromic devices (ECDs) are devices that change color and optical properties under an applied voltage and have widespread uses in smart windows, displays, and wearables. Typically, ECDs function through an electrochemical redox reaction, in which a change in voltage induces the transport of ions between the cathode and anode. This, in turn, changes the material's light absorption properties by transporting ion into or out of the electrochromic layer resulting in either a colored or bleached state that is sustained without the need for continuous power. One major challenge in the development of ECDs is the limitation of color contrast in these devices, providing only shades of a single color instead of a full, continuous visible spectrum. This restricted color range limits the versatility of ECDs in applications that require rich color displays. An approach to overcome this limitation explores the use of structural color, in which color arises from the interaction of light with the nanoscale structures of particles. Structural color results from optical phenomena such as interference, diffraction, and scattering from nanostructures, allowing the color of light to be tuned by adjusting structural parameters such as interparticle spacing. Therefore, integrating structural color mechanisms into electrochromic architecture offers a promising pathway toward ECDs with a broader color palette. By incorporating nanostructures whose particle spacing can be electrically modulated into ECDs, it becomes possible to dynamically tune coloration across the continuous visible spectrum. Such systems have potential in expanding the functionality of ECDs for next-generation adaptive displays and optical technologies.

title: The Creeping Return of Antiquated Views on Womanhood: How Gen-Z Women Experience the Socio-Political Climate
abstract: This study aims to understand the impacts of the current socio-political climate on Gen-Z women's emotions, identity, and interpersonal dynamics. Focusing this study on Northwestern's campus ensures that accurate patterns and results can be concluded while keeping as many variables as possible consistent. To examine the impact of the socio-political climate on young women, I conducted 15 semi-structured and openended interviews with individuals who identified as female, were eligible to vote in the 2024 election, and were upperclassmen at Northwestern University. Findings revealed significant trends in the influence of the socio-political on young women's every day and personal life. Young women cited feeling distressed about the overall future of the world, specifically in the regression of gender equity and inclusion. Feelings of emotional suppression were also common and deliberately used to create mental distance from the political landscape. Many young women described feeling solidarity among themselves, insinuating that they felt more confident and comfortable around other women. In some instances, women had distorted self-perceptions of themselves, created by a heightened hyper-awareness of social perception. Finally, participants expressed negative sentiment and difficulty in connection with those of opposing ideologies. Many described a physical and emotional gap that has been created between young men and women, emphasizing the difficulty for women to form close and intimate relationships with men. Future directions for this research should focus on comparing the emotional, identity forming, and interpersonal impacts the sociopolitical climate has had for Gen-Z men.

title: Automated X-ray Analysis of Ice Formation in Drosophila Larvae
abstract: In Earth's coldest environments, organisms survive sub-zero temperatures by producing antifreeze proteins (AFPs) that control ice formation and prevent cellular damage. The snowfly Chionea alexandriana expresses a hypothetical anti-freeze protein, CaAFP, but its mechanism of ice binding and crystal growth regulation remains unclear. We developed an X-ray diffraction (XRD) assay to probe the impact of CaAFP expressed in Drosophila melanogaster larvae on the freezing point. Our objective was to determine the impact of CaAFP on crystallographic parameters of ice crystals as a first step of determining its mechanism. To facilitate the analysis of XRD patterns (280-240 K, 1K intervals), we developed an automated Python pipeline to simultaneously fit the (100), (002), and (101) reflections with Pseudo-Voigt profiles. Peak parameters were extracted separately from the multi-peak fits and pooled across temperatures within each sample group prior to statistical comparison. No significant differences in peak positions or amplitudes were observed, indicating unchanged lattice parameters. However, all three reflections showed broader full width half maximum (FWHM) in CaAFP-expressing samples. The FWHM of the (100) reflection in CaAFP-expressing larvae (FWHM1 = 0.181) was significantly larger than in WT larvae (p = 3.36 10-7) consistent with decrease in crystallite size or an increase in lattice strain, or a combination thereof. Our findings reveal that CaAFP directly reshapes the crystallographic parameters of ice crystals formed in vivo, supporting direct ice binding mechanism. The approach further establishes a quantitative framework for studying ice-protein interactions and advances cryopreservation and the design of bioinspired antifreeze materials.

title: Exploring the Relationship between Adverse Childhood Experiences and the Development of Coping Strategies in Young Adults
abstract: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) can be categorised as potentially traumatic incidents that occur before the age of 17. These are well established as predictors of long term negative outcomes. However, little is known about the processes through which ACEs lead to these outcomes, or why individuals with similar environmental (ACEs and Positive Childhood Experiences (PCEs)) and intrinsic factors (personality traits) may have vastly different trajectories. No study has integrated these factors into a single model, and therefore the current study shifts focus from outcomes to mechanisms, examining coping as a key pathway linking early experiences to later outcomes. Participants (N=378) completed measures of ACEs, coping behaviour, PCEs, and personality traits. Regression analyses showed that ACEs positively predicted all coping styles including avoidant (maladaptive), emotion-focused, and problem-focused (generally adaptive) coping. Coping increased at low-moderate ACE levels and plateaued at higher ACE exposure, which suggests a nonlinear trend of cumulative risk. PCEs were associated with greater adaptive coping and lower avoidant coping. Extraversion and conscientiousness were linked to adaptive coping, while neuroticism was linked to maladaptive coping. In cumulative risk models, ACEs explained additional variance beyond personality in avoidant emotional and problemfocused coping, while PCEs contributed to adaptive coping. No interaction effects were observed. PCEs and personality appear to be independently associated with more adaptive coping. These findings suggest that ACEs influence the overall organisation of coping mechanisms and meaningfully contribute to their development along with critical factors of positive experiences and personality that could inform future interventions.

title: Understanding Causes of Altered Imitation in Autism: A Novel Hypothesis
abstract: Imitation is important for learning motor and social skills, both of which are often altered in autistic individuals. Prior work suggests that autistic children have more difficulty imitating gestures when multiple joints move at the same time, but it is not clear whether these differences are driven by coordinating multiple movement elements versus overall motor complexity. This study tested whether breaking gestures into step-by-step parts differentially improves imitation in autism and examined the roles of motor and non-motor processes. Typically developing (n = 70) and autistic (n = 54) children (ages 8-12) completed two experimental tasks. In Experiment 1, they imitated 20 novel gestures shown either all at once or step-by-step, and performance was scored based on element-wise accuracy. In Experiment 2, they completed a delayed-match-to-sample judgment task to measure non-motor processing. Step-bystep presentation improved imitation and reduced group differences (condition diagnosis interaction, t(114) = 2.1, p = .042), but a gap between groups remained. In the judgment task, there was no effect of presentation style, though autistic children still differed from neurotypical children. Mediation analysis showed that non-motor processes explained about 34% of the group difference in imitation. Overall, breaking gestures into steps reduces imitation differences, but does not fully close the gap, suggesting that interventions which scaffold actions into sequential components may improve performance but should also directly target motor coordination. These results also suggest that motor processes are a primary contributor to imitation differences in autism and may be an important target for intervention.

title: Interpreting Justice: How Legal Practitioners Conceptualize Fairness, Justice, and their Role in the Changing Illinois Criminal Record Relief Landscape
abstract: Among Illinois's 12.7 million residents, approximately 3 million have a criminal record, which can restrict access to employment, housing, and educational opportunities. The Clean Slate Act represents a significant shift in how the state approaches criminal record relief. Little is known about how legal professionals will navigate this new landscape, not only in terms of procedure, but in conceptions of their own roles within the system. This thesis draws on seven semi-structured interviews to examine how legal aid lawyers make sense of justice, fairness, and professional responsibility within Illinois's evolving expungement and sealing system, engaging in analysis through open coding and a Grounded Theory approach. Attorneys' conceptions of justice emerge through three interconnected themes, each reflecting a core tension they must navigate. First, lawyers articulate abstract ideals of justice while simultaneously confronting a criminal legal system they view as inherently complex and overly punitive. Second, they experience criminal record relief as a transformative but imperfect remedy to the system. Third, lawyers consistently frame their work in moral terms, describing an obligation to clients, a responsibility to advocate, and a commitment to educating clients, even as policy change brings both hope and skepticism. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how policy reforms are implemented on the ground, examining how well-intentioned legislation can produce unintended consequences or inconsistencies in practice. Lawyers are responsible for interpreting and navigating these policies, so academic analysis of their experiences is critical to inform more effective and equitable future reforms.

title: Repurposing ALOX5 Inhibition for Psoriasis Treatment
abstract: Psoriasis is a common autoimmune, inflammatory disorder affecting 2-3% of the global population. Plaque psoriasis, the most common manifestation of the disease, is linked with soreness, joint pains, and dry, itchy patches of skin. While the disease's pathogenesis has been largely attributed to IL-17 secretion by T-helper 17 (Th17) cells to amplify keratinocyte-mediated skin inflammation, the underlying intracellular signaling mechanisms within keratinocytes remain incompletely defined. This gap in mechanistic understanding has constrained therapeutic development, with current treatments largely limited to costly systemic biologics that can carry significant side effects. To identify novel regulators of keratinocyte responses to IL-17, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in primary human epidermal keratinocytes, focusing on genetic regulators of IL-17 receptor A (IL17RA), a central node in psoriatic inflammation. This screen identified arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5) as a top candidate. We demonstrate that ALOX5 functions as a lipid mediator that stabilizes IL17RA expression at the cell surface, thereby amplifying IL-17-driven inflammatory signaling. Importantly, targeting ALOX5 with Zileuton, an FDA-approved drug currently used to treat asthma, showed strong inhibitory effects towards IL17RA in keratinocytes. Zileuton also demonstrated potent therapeutic effects when applied topically to a mouse model of imiquimod-induced psoriasis, performing comparably to existing FDA-approved anti-IL17RA antibody treatments for plaque psoriasis. Overall, topical Zileuton suppressed pathogenic Th17 responses, promoted anti-inflammatory macrophage polarization, and normalized epidermal hyperproliferation. Together, these findings identify ALOX5 as a previously unrecognized regulator of the IL-17 signaling axis and highlight the potential of repurposing Zileuton as a targeted therapeutic strategy for psoriasis.

title: Gender Differences in Self-Perceptions of ADHD Diagnosis: Identity, Relief, and Stigma
abstract: Despite its prevalence, there is little research examining how individuals make sense of their Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnoses. The purpose of this study was to explore the relationship between gender and self-perceptions of receiving an ADHD diagnosis through two domains: positive appraisals (selfunderstanding and sense of relief) and negative appraisals (stigma). Age of diagnosis was also examined as a potential explanatory factor. A sample of 364 young adults from the U.S. with self-reported formal ADHD diagnoses was surveyed through Prolific on their experiences following diagnosis. The results indicated that women were significantly more likely than men to experience self-understanding and relief as a result of getting diagnosed. Age at diagnosis was partially related to this, with later diagnosed individuals reporting higher levels of self-understanding and relief, but gender differences remained even when age was considered. There were no significant gender differences observed with stigma, though individuals diagnosed before their adolescence reported higher levels of stigma. These findings underscore the importance of considering gender and diagnostic timing when exploring the psychological impact of an ADHD diagnosis. On a broader scale, these results reinforce the need to address gender disparities in ADHD diagnosis, potentially driven by diagnostic criteria and expectations that center on a prototypical, male presentation. Differences in appraisal may reflect the greater distress experienced by girls and women as a result of years going undiagnosed.

title: Identification of Host Ranges, Receptors, and Defense Genes For the JG024 Phage in Clinical Isolates of Pseudomonas Aeruginosa (PA)
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a major cause of hospital-acquired infection and can rapidly develop antibiotic resistance. Bacteriophage (phage) therapy offers a promising and highly specific alternative treatment. However, PA possesses diverse and complex anti-phage defense systems, many of which remain uncharacterized. Understanding the mechanisms by which PA resists phage is critical to developing effective phage therapies. Identifying specific genes and receptors responsible for phage susceptibility or resistance would allow targeted strategies to enhance phage therapy success. In this experiment, we investigate phage-host receptor interactions and use cloning-based approaches to introduce candidate defense genes to uncover these mechanisms. To explore phage defense mechanisms in PA, we first determined the host range of 215 PA clinical isolates against the lytic phage JG024. For a phage to lyse its target, it must first bind bacterial surface receptors. The O11 and O3 lipopolysaccharide antigens and the type IV pili component PilA5 were identified as candidates, showing statistical correlations with JG024 susceptibility in bioinformatic analyses. Preliminary results suggest a positive correlation between the O11 antigen and JG024 susceptibility. To determine whether these receptors mediate phage binding, qPCR is being used to quantify JG024 binding to isolates expressing each receptor. Bioinformatic analysis also identified genes statistically correlated with phage susceptibility across isolates, from which a candidate defense gene was selected for introduction into a phage-susceptible PA reference strain. This gene did not confer phage resistance; however, ongoing qPCR binding assays and defense gene investigation aim to inform future strategies for optimizing phage therapy against PA.

title: Development of a Fluorescence-Based Endomicroscope System for Quantitative Assessment of Pediatric Aspiration
abstract: Aspiration, the accidental inhalation of foreign material into the lungs, is a severe, yet critically understudied, clinical danger for pediatric and neurologically impaired patients that can lead to life-threatening respiratory complications. Current diagnostic methods, such as videofluoroscopic swallow studies, only provide indirect, qualitative assessments. They lack the sensitivity to directly visualize or measure aspirated material at the microscopic level. To address this gap, we present a proof-of-concept fluorescence endomicroscope designed to directly detect and quantify aspirated fluorescent particles (microspheres) within lung tissue. Our system utilizes a specialized optical setup, featuring a broadband LED, wavelength filters, and a highresolution sensor, to illuminate the tissue and capture the fluorescence of these microscopic particles, acting as a proxy for aspiration severity. We successfully demonstrated that this system reliably visualizes microspheres in lung tissue samples. By applying an image analysis algorithm, we quantified particle density, providing an objective metric of the aspiration burden. Experimental results showed that while thicker, physiologically relevant tissue reduced image contrast due to light scattering, the particles remained clearly identifiable. System resolution easily distinguished individual 10-micrometer particles, and sampling analysis confirmed that this performance is limited by optical physics rather than sensor constraints. These findings establish fluorescence endomicroscopy as a viable method for directly visualizing and measuring microscale aspiration. This platform introduces a vital shift from subjective observation to precise, quantitative measurement, offering a powerful new framework for early diagnosis, severity grading, targeted treatment monitoring in highly vulnerable patient populations, and general aspiration study.

title: Feedback-based Training and Musicality Teach People to Detect Deepfake Speech
abstract: Recent advancements in AI text-to-speech systems have enabled the creation of highquality deepfake voices increasingly indistinguishable from real voices. These deepfakes have been used to impersonate and defraud people, yet few studies have looked at ways to teach people to detect deepfakes. This study sought to determine whether feedback-based teaching paradigms and musicality confer improvements in deepfake detection. 50 participants (of either gender) listened to sentences produced either by a human speaker or an AI-generated voice clone before judging each sentence as real or fake. After judging these sentences for ~10 minutes, participants underwent a ~20 minute training block where they received feedback (correct/incorrect) based on their answers, before returning to a post-training block identical to the pre-training one. Participants also underwent a musical skills test. Behaviorally, participants demonstrated poor discriminatory sensitivity prior to the training block and improved sensitivity after the training, revealing that even short feedback-oriented training procedures can be used to teach deepfake detection, contrasting recent research saying that short training sessions do not lead to improvements in deepfake detection. Additionally, musicality and rhythm-based skills were correlated with deepfake detection and larger improvements in that detection after training. These findings establish a framework for effective deepfake detection pedagogy, a step towards reducing the societal threats posed by deepfake voice fraud. Understanding that musicality in specific leads some listeners to detect deepfakes better than others reveals tractable perceptual mechanisms that can be leveraged to design further research into deepfake detection training interventions.

title: Baseball's Highest Stakes Situation and a Decision Error Three Decades Deep
abstract: It's the bottom of the ninth inning, two outs, bases loaded. The conventional instinct in baseball is to swing at a hitter's count. This paper argues that instinct has been wrong for at least three decades and that the sport has not corrected it. With bases loaded and two outs, a walk simultaneously scores a run and preserves the identical threat for the next batter, who then faces the same high-leverage situation from a fresh count. This self-reinforcing property means that patience compounds across consecutive plate appearances in a way that attacking any individual pitch cannot match. This paper formalizes this using an augmented Markov Decision Process applied across 192 possible game states. The model recommends taking the pitch at 10 of 12 count states in a tied game and 11 of 12 when trailing by one run. Against 35 years of Major League Baseball pitch by pitch data, the gap between optimal and observed behavior is large and entirely unidirectional. Batters over-swing at every non-two-strike count, at costs reaching 19 percentage points of win probability at the single most expensive state. Not one of the 48 count-and-deficit combinations in the data shows underswinging. The gap has not narrowed from 1990 to 2024, surviving the full analytics revolution. The finding connects to the behavioral economics literature on action bias and suggests that trained motor responses, unlike deliberate decisions, resist strategic correction.

title: Application of Red Fluorescent PLGA Microspheres for Quantitative Assessment of Pediatric Aspiration
abstract: Pediatric aspiration is a clinically significant condition that can lead to chronic lung injury, infection, and long-term respiratory complications, yet current diagnostic methods such as videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) and fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) remain largely qualitative and do not quantify aspiration severity. This project aimed to address this gap by developing a microsphere-based approach to enable quantitative assessment of aspiration. Red fluorescent poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) microspheres were used as surrogate tracers to model aspirated material due to their biocompatibility, controlled size, and improved detectability compared to free dyes. The use of red fluorescence was selected to reduce interference from natural tissue autofluorescence in the airway. The system was evaluated across multiple experimental models, including fixed pig trachea, fresh murine lung and tracheal tissue, and a New Zealand rabbit airway perfusion model to simulate aspiration under physiologically relevant conditions. Known concentrations of microspheres were introduced to assess detectability and quantifiability across conditions. Results demonstrated that microspheres could be reliably detected and quantified in fresh tissue, with higher concentrations producing clear, countable signals and improved signal-to-background contrast. These findings support the feasibility of using microspheres as quantitative tracers for aspiration and establish a foundation for correlating particle distribution with aspiration severity. This approach has the potential to improve diagnostic precision, enable objective severity grading, and support better clinical decision-making in the management of pediatric aspiration.

title: Targeting poison exon splicing to modulate CHD2 protein production
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) can be caused by changes in certain genes. One of these genes, CHD2, helps control DNA packaging and gene activation. Harmful changes in CHD2 reduce the amount of CHD2 protein the body makes, which can lead to conditions such as epilepsy, intellectual disability, and autism. There are currently no treatments that directly address the underlying cause, and traditional gene therapy is difficult because CHD2 is too large to target with standard methods. CHD2 contains a short poison exon, a segment of RNA that, if included in the final transcript, causes the RNA to be destroyed before it can make protein. This lowers the overall amount of CHD2 protein. We propose that reducing inclusion of this poison exon could naturally increase CHD2 levels. To test this idea, we will use engineered cells that express a modified protein fused to a splicing factor. Guide RNAs can direct this complex to the poison exon to change how the exon is spliced into the transcript. We will measure and sequence CHD2 RNA to determine whether targeting the poison exon decreases its inclusion and increases overall transcript levels. We aim to demonstrate that adjusting splicing can raise CHD2 protein levels, and that splicebased approaches may offer a promising method of treating disorders caused by genes that cannot be targeted with conventional gene therapy.

title: Linking niche diversity to phylogenetic relatedness in freshwater bacteria assemblies
abstract: Aquatic bacteria are critical to the health of lake ecosystems because they aid in the cycling of nutrients and removal of pollutants. Current methods to study these bacteria rely heavily on taxonomic classification. Taxonomic classification works well for understanding environmental roles of higher organisms, for example plants are primary producers and carnivorous animals are predators. However, these classifications are less useful for bacteria, whose ecological role may be more variable, because they do not directly reflect the function of these bacteria in lake ecosystems. To better understand the relationship between taxonomic classification and ecological function in aquatic bacteria, we use two decades of publicly available bacterial DNA sequencing data from Lake Mendota in Madison, WI. By analyzing all the genes present in these environmental samples, we compare functional gene diversity patterns in 10 groups of bacteria. Results indicate that groups have variable diversity levels, meaning some bacterial groups may perform a wider array of ecological functions than others despite having the same taxonomic classification. Specific motility and phage-related genes show differential presence patterns across different groups, which present a possible explanation for this variation. Abstract mathematical analysis called topological data analysis further indicates complicated dynamics in bacterial diversity. Together, these results demonstrate that genetically identified groups have different patterns in functional adaptability, indicating a need for revision in the current taxonomy model for one that accounts for the entire genome. Future efforts will be needed to validate these data across a broader array of environments and with more accurate sequencing.

title: How Trait-Mindfulness and Working Alliance Predict Treatment Engagement in an Adolescent Mindfulness Study
abstract: As various interventions for mental health conditions have been developed, engagement with such treatments and their homework between sessions has been linked to numerous key outcomes, including reductions in symptoms of depression and anxiety, and signs of overall therapeutic change. The aspects of trait-mindfulness and client-rated working alliance have been shown to predict such engagement in an intervention, but gaps still exist, especially with regards to examining adolescent populations and for more accessible interventions that do not necessarily involve a professional clinician. The present research thus utilizes data from the Youth Mindful Awareness Program (YMAP) study that delivers two evidence-based interventions, one emphasizing mindfulness and the other focusing on expressive writing. This project also uses trained undergraduate coaches and focuses on adolescent populations rated as being at higher risk for developing depression and anxiety. In the current study, the variables of trait-mindfulness, measured at baseline, and working alliance, measured at the midpoint of the study, are tested to see if they predict engagement in the YMAP study across both conditions. Here, engagement is defined as completion of the assigned between-session practices for the 9 weeks of the study. Results of a multiple regression analysis showed a non-significant relationship between these variables and engagement. Recommendations are given for future directions and studies that can possibly better represent the effects of working alliance and traitmindfulness and contribute to existing theories.

title: Signs of Change: A Cross-Cultural Exploration of Minority Language Revitalization through Linguistic Landscape
abstract: Global language loss is occurring at an unprecedented rate, with profound cultural, intellectual, and social consequences. Language revitalization seeks to counter historical and ongoing forces of marginalization, yet its success is often difficult to measure in practice. This study examines the visibility of minority and Indigenous languages in multilingual, post-colonial urban contexts through a mixed-methods approach, combining semi-structured interviews with ethnographic observation and photographic documentation of public signage. The analysis of the linguistic landscape of Wales, South Africa, Singapore, the Philippines, and New Zealand provides a tangible metric for assessing the material presence of these languages, while interviews contextualize patterns of visibility within local policy frameworks, community attitudes, and sociolinguistic realities. Findings reveal how public signage reflects and reinforces language hierarchies, highlights discrepancies between revitalization ideals and implementation, and offers insight into the role of Indigenous and local knowledge in shaping language visibility. By linking linguistic theory with material and social evidence, this study contributes to understanding the interplay between language policy, public space, and efforts toward linguistic and cultural sustainability.

title: From Scarcity to Solidarity: Mutual Aid as a Pathway to Food Sovereignty and Urban Resilience in Chennai, India
abstract: In the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, 23.1% of the population is undernourished, according to estimates from the Global Hunger Index, despite the state's robust welfare programs. In an urban area like Chennai, food insecurity is compounded by poverty, gender inequality, and caste apartheid. Additionally, extreme weather driven by climate change has caused localized food shortages that disproportionately affect marginalized groups. In the face of these overlapping inequalities, mutual aid may empower local people to reclaim their right to food produced through ecologically sustainable means. Mutual aid refers to a collective exchange of resources between community members for reciprocal benefit. This presentation investigates how mutual aid networks in Chennai organize to create pathways to food sovereignty and urban resilience. Through interviews with members of grassroots organizations, including a climate justice non-profit, an urban farming initiative, and a food re-distribution network, this study unpacks how mutual aid can be understood in a South Asian context, specifically in relation to caste apartheid and gender inequality. This study further examines how these networks engage with notions of reciprocity while challenging or reproducing charitable logics. Women's self-help groups (SHGs) and grassroots organizations were found to be significant models of mutual aid in Chennai. These organizations engage in the local production and distribution of nourishing food. Such structures support the creation of green spaces and the reduction of food waste. These systems of community care operate in democratic ways that empower lower-income women and center caste-oppressed and tribal communities in aid distribution efforts.

title: Synthesis of Cyanine-labeled Peptides for AuNP Labeling and Lysosomal Enzyme Detection
abstract: Lysosomal enzymes, known as cathepsins, facilitate the controlled degradation and recycling of cellular proteins, which is necessary to maintain cellular balance and function. In many cancers, cathepsins become overactive and begin degrading components of the extracellular matrix, the structural network that keeps cells in place. This breakdown enables tumor cells to invade neighboring tissue and form malignant growths. Detecting cathepsin activity in real time is therefore important for diagnosis, monitoring disease progression, and evaluating therapeutic response. Fluorescent imaging probes can serve as indicators of enzyme activity, as their emission can be altered depending on their incorporation into a molecule. However, conventional probes emit light continuously, regardless of whether the target enzyme is active, which produces high background fluorescence and makes it difficult to distinguish activity from noise. This project aims to develop an enzyme-activated ("turn-on") fluorescence probe by attaching specially designed cyanine dyes to gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) through a cathepsin-cleavable peptide. When this peptide is connected to the AuNP, the dye will be held close to the gold surface, where its fluorescence is quenched (appears "off"). When cathepsin cuts the dye-AuNP linker, the dye is released and its fluorescence intensity increases. The goal of this project is to synthesize and evaluate a small library of these cyanine dye constructs, compare how structural variations of linkers influence performance, and determine which probe designs produce a strong and reliable fluorescence activation signal.

title: Isolation and Characterization of Seven Novel Psuedomonas aeruginosa Bacteriophages
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa)is a Gram-negative bacterium responsible for many hospital acquired infections that are particularly difficult to treat due to high levels of antibiotic resistance. As the number of multidrug-resistant strains continues to rise, interest in alternative forms of treatment, like bacteriophage (phage) therapy, has been renewed. Phage therapy involves the use of bacteriophages, or viruses that infect bacteria, to target and kill the pathogen of interest. However, due to the overwhelming abundance and diversity of phages, further characterization is needed for reliable clinical use. In this study, seven novel bacteriophages (p001-p007) were isolated from wastewater that were active against multidrug-resistant Pa. After enrichment and purification, the host range of each phage, as well as that of three previously isolated phages (e.g. JG024, phiKZ), was tested using a panel of antibiotic-resistant clinical isolates (n=51). For each phage-strain combination, efficiency of plating (EOP) was calculated by comparing plaque formation on the test strain to the strain from which each phage was isolated. Host range varied widely among phages, with one phage infecting only one additional strain (n=2) while another infected almost half (n=25) of all stains tested. The turbidity of plaques did not correlate with EOP, suggesting that plaque morphology is not a dependable indicator of productive infection. To further characterize each original phage, genomes were sequenced and transmission electron microscopy was used to examine phage morphology. Overall, this study expands on current understanding of phage diversity and provides preliminary data for future therapeutic applications.

title: Improving Medical Training to Address Health Literacy Gaps in Middle Eastern North African Americans
abstract: Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) Americans are currently classified as White in U.S. datasets, which obscures meaningful health disparities and limits the ability to study their specific healthcare needs. Health literacy (HL), defined as the ability to understand and use health information, is a critical determinant of health outcomes. This study aims to evaluate differences in HL between MENA Americans and White individuals and to highlight the need for more accurate demographic classification. We conducted a retrospective analysis using data from the NIH All of Us database. Health literacy was measured using the BRIEF-3 scale, where scores 9 indicate inadequate HL. Participants were stratified by race, education, income, and age. Statistical analyses included one-way ANOVA to assess differences across subgroups (p & 0.05 considered significant) and to evaluate overall differences between racial groups. Results showed that HL confidence increased with higher education, income, and age for both groups. However, White participants consistently reported higher HL scores than MENA participants across all subgroups. These differences were statistically significant, with strong interactions between race and education, income, and age. Distributional analysis further confirmed persistent disparities, with MENA individuals more likely to have lower HL scores. These findings demonstrate a clear disparity in health literacy that is currently masked by racial misclassification. Recognizing MENA as a distinct demographic group is essential for improving data accuracy, informing targeted interventions, and promoting health equity in medical training which is the primary focus of this study.

title: The Role of Self-Concept Clarity in Decision-Making Under Time Pressure and Groupthink
abstract: Companies often face high-stakes decisions in which uncertainty, time pressure, and hierarchical structures can shape how individuals contribute to group outcomes. In such contexts, groupthink can lead individuals to align with authority figures, reducing overall decision quality. Although situational pressures are known to influence conformity, less is known about how individual differences such as self-concept clarity (SCC) affect willingness to voice independent opinions. Prior research on SCC has largely focused on individual rather than group decision-making. This study examines how SCC interacts with groupthink and time pressure to influence decision-making and argument quality. Participants (N = 425) were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: high time pressure with groupthink, low time pressure with groupthink, or low time pressure without groupthink. Participants participated in a simulated decision stimuli regarding whether to recall a defective medical device. We found that groupthink significantly influenced decision outcomes: participants were more likely to align with the CEO's recommendation under groupthink regardless of time pressure (x2(1, 285) = 64.66, p & 0.001). Groupthink also reduced argument strength (v = 0.133, p = 0.006). Although SCC did not have a direct effect on argument strength (v = 0.002, p = 0.963), it significantly moderated responses under groupthink conditions (v = 0.116, p = 0.016), such that individuals with higher SCC produced stronger arguments when social pressure was present. These findings suggest that while groupthink drives conformity, self-concept clarity functions as a psychological buffer that supports independent judgment under social pressure.

title: Juvenile Regulatory T Cells Exhibit Decreased Capacity to Suppress Inflammation During Severe Influenza Pneumonia
abstract: Healthy children are more likely than adults to develop severe viral pneumonia, which can lead to long-term impairments in cardiopulmonary function. Our group demonstrated that juvenile mice exhibit prolonged inflammation following influenza A virus (IAV) infection compared to adults, despite equivalent viral clearance. In adults, regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress inflammation and promote tissue repair, in part by suppressing conventional T cell (Tcon) proliferation. We hypothesize that juvenile Treg reparative function is impaired during IAV infection, contributing to prolonged inflammation and aberrant lung repair. To test this, the suppressive capacities of Tregs from adult and juvenile mice were compared using lymphocyte suppression assays. Juvenile Foxp3DTR mice were infected with a sublethal titer of IAV and treated with diphtheria toxin to deplete Tregs. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) IL-6 and Amphiregulin (AREG) were quantified using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and lung immune cells were enumerated using flow cytometry. Lungs were assessed by H&E and immunofluorescent microscopy staining for lung injury and repair markers. Juvenile Tregs suppressed Tcon proliferation less effectively than adult Tregs. Treg-sufficient and Treg-deficient juvenile mice failed to reach the growth potential of uninfected mice. Depleting Tregs did not alter BALF IL-6, neutrophil, or AREG levels. Both Treg-sufficient and Treg-deficient mice exhibited severe injury, Krt5+ regions, and Krt8hi cells consistent with abnormal alveolar architecture and repair. These findings suggest juvenile Tregs are insufficient to mitigate inflammation and promote repair during severe viral pneumonia. Further understanding of juvenile Treg function may inform strategies to improve pediatric recovery from severe respiratory infection.

title: Neurotensin circuit regulation under approach-avoidance conflict
abstract: In nature, seeking rewards is essential for survival, but rarely comes without risk. Food, shelter, and social connection are all important rewards that can require risk taking. How the brain decides when a reward is worth seeking is an essential question that underlies important disorders such as anxiety and substance use disorders (SUDs). This project investigates how Neurotensin (NT), a neuropeptide highly expressed within the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), modulates reward and aversive behavior. To study this, our lab developed the Approach-Avoidance Conflict (Conflict) Task in which mice are trained to seek a sucrose reward while receiving progressively stronger foot shocks, an environment that weighs a decision between desire and risk. We used video-based scoring to quantify mouse risk assessment behaviors, reactivity to foot-shocks, and freezing. In addition, projections from NT neurons located in the PVT to nearby regions were mapped in the mouse brain.
